t: Number of Days in a Month — Editorial
o: We must return how many days a given month of a given year has. Most months have fixed lengths (31 or 30 days); only February varies, depending on whether the year is a leap year. A leap year is divisible by 4, except century years, which must be divisible by 400. For example, month=7 always has 31 days; February in 2000 (divisible by 400) has 29 days, while February in 1900 (divisible by 100 but not 400) has 28. The tiny constraints mean any direct lookup/branching solution is fine — no loops or complex algorithms are needed.
k: Only February's length depends on the year; all other months have fixed day counts.
Leap-year rule: divisible by 4 and (not divisible by 100 or divisible by 400).
A lookup table plus one leap-year check solves the problem in O(1).

a.n: Approach 1: Lookup Table + Leap Year Check
a.i: Store the standard day counts for the 12 months in an array, then adjust February to 29 when the year is a leap year. The leap condition `year % 4 == 0 && (year % 100 != 0 || year % 400 == 0)` exactly captures the Gregorian calendar rule, which is valid since the constraints guarantee years >= 1583.
s: Check if the year is a leap year: divisible by 4 and (not by 100 or by 400).
If it is a leap year, set days[1] = 29.
a.t: O(1) — constant array access and arithmetic.
a.sp: O(1) — a fixed-size array of 12 integers.

a.i: Most languages provide calendar utilities that already handle leap years correctly. We can ask for the last day of the month directly (e.g., Python's calendar.monthrange) or compute the number of days as the difference between the first of this month and the first of the next month using date arithmetic.
s: Query the length of the given month for the given year.
a.sp: O(1) — only a few date objects/values.

w: In an interview, present Approach 1: it shows you know the Gregorian leap-year rule and needs no library knowledge. Use Approach 2 if the interviewer allows built-ins and you want minimal code. Common pitfalls: forgetting the century exception (1900 is not a leap year but 2000 is), misremembering which months have 30 vs 31 days, and off-by-one indexing on the month array. Edge cases to test: February in 2000 (29), 1900 (28), 1996 (29), and boundary years 1583 and 2100. Likely follow-ups: count days between two dates, determine the day of week for a date, or validate an arbitrary date.
